newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian inflation seen calm for now despite Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Indian inflation seen calm for now despite Iraq.

text.p: Higher oil prices triggered by U.S. missile attacks against Iraq are unlikely to spur inflation in India in the short term, but could cause concern if there is no decline next month, analysts said on Thursday.

"It is too short-term a situation. Unless we contract large imports, there will be no inflationary pressure," Shashanka Bhide, an economist at National Council of Applied Economic Research, told Reuters.
India's inflation rate, measured by the wholesale price index, was 5.54 percent on August 17. This compared with 8.0 percent at the end of 1995 and 8.50 percent in August 1995.
India imports about 40 percent of its oil and product needs. This cost around $6.5 billion and accounts for just over 20 percent of the country's total import bill.
The analysts said inflation could increase if oil prices remained at current high levels for more than one month.

"Currently, the expectation is of higher oil prices. Purchases have to be made at higher prices from now onwards and this was not built into government's calculations of fiscal deficit," said Aashish Pitale, an analyst of ICICI Securities and Finance Co Ltd.
The U.S. launched a second wave of missiles against military targets in southern Iraq on Wednesday in retaliation for Iraqi military intervention in the country's Kurdish north.
India's economy, particularly its balance of payments, is vulnerable to swings in global oil prices.

A jump in oil prices during the 1990-91 Gulf War triggered a crisis in India's balance of payments. But analysts said India, with foreign exchange reserves totalling about $18.0 billion, was in a better position now to deal with oil price increases.
India's fiscal deficit was 5.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1995/96 (April-March) and is projected at 5.0 percent in the year ending next March.
Senior Oil Ministry and state-owned petroleum company officials met in New Delhi on Thursday to assess the impact on the oil import bill following the attacks on Iraq.
"There are a few ships carrying crude as well as products leaving the Middle East this week that will be subjected to higher prices," an industry official said.
India's imports of 22-to-23 million tonnes of crude and 16 million tonnes of refined oil products cost about $6.5 billion in 1995.
